variants.title: Run the dataset lifecycle
variants.context: The dataset lifecycle is four release decisions. Register sources with origin, owner, schema, event time, allowed uses, and retention. Build and label examples with versioned point-in-time-safe transformations. Validate and freeze by checking structure, distributions, labels, slices, leakage, and policy before signing a manifest. Then trace and maintain the release through the model runs that consume it.
variants.prompt: A team builds its first fraud training dataset from payment events and analyst reviews. Put the lifecycle stages in order.

items.text: Link the training runs to the release and monitor the data behavior it produces in production.
Build and label examples with versioned point-in-time-safe transformations, preserving the rubric and who produced each label.
Validate structure, distributions, duplicates, labels, slices, leakage, and policy, then sign a manifest once the gates pass.
Register the payment and review sources with origin, owner, schema, event time, sampling method, allowed uses, and retention.

variants.hint: Nothing can be frozen before it has been derived, and nothing derived before its sources are known.
variants.explanation: Register, derive, release, operate. Each stage emits the evidence the next one depends on.

variants.title: Run the dataset lifecycle
variants.context: The dataset lifecycle is four release decisions. Register sources with origin, owner, schema, event time, allowed uses, and retention. Build and label examples with versioned point-in-time-safe transformations. Validate and freeze by checking structure, distributions, labels, slices, leakage, and policy before signing a manifest. Then trace and maintain the release through the model runs that consume it.
variants.prompt: Annotators re-adjudicate 3,000 disputed labels and the dataset must be rebuilt around them. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Sign a new release identity and record which model runs should move to it.
Confirm the label source, rubric version, and adjudication policy that produced the corrected votes.
Rebuild the examples so the corrected labels join their features as of the original prediction time.
Rerun every gate on the new candidate and compare it with the previous known-good release.

variants.hint: A corrected label is still a labeled observation under a versioned process.
variants.explanation: Corrections re-enter the same lifecycle. They produce a new release rather than an edit to the signed one.

variants.title: Run the dataset lifecycle
variants.context: The dataset lifecycle is four release decisions. Register sources with origin, owner, schema, event time, allowed uses, and retention. Build and label examples with versioned point-in-time-safe transformations. Validate and freeze by checking structure, distributions, labels, slices, leakage, and policy before signing a manifest. Then trace and maintain the release through the model runs that consume it.
variants.prompt: A vendor feed is added as a new source for an existing dataset. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Check the candidate for new missingness, duplicates, slice shifts, and policy violations the feed introduces.
Publish a compatibility note with the new release so consumers know what changed in meaning.
Join the vendor fields into examples using the same point-in-time rules the existing sources follow.
Record the vendor's origin, license, schema, event time, allowed uses, and how corrections arrive.

variants.hint: A new source changes the population before it changes the metrics.
variants.explanation: Adding a source is a release, not a config change, because it alters coverage, policy scope, and feature meaning.

variants.title: Trace a removal through lineage
variants.context: Lineage answers both directions: what produced this model, and what depends on this source. When a source is corrected, expires, or becomes disallowed, resolve its identity to affected examples and releases, determine which model runs consumed them and where those artifacts are deployed, apply the governing response, and preserve an audit record without retaining prohibited payloads.
variants.prompt: A customer withdraws consent for the records that produced training examples. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Preserve an audit record of the request, scope, decision, and completed actions without retaining the prohibited payload.
Apply the governing response: remove, rebuild, retrain, restrict, or document an approved exception.
Resolve the customer's source identity to every affected example and released dataset.
Determine which model runs consumed those releases and where their artifacts are deployed.

variants.hint: You cannot decide the response before you know what depends on the source.
variants.explanation: Lineage makes the impact discoverable so an accountable owner can decide. Automatic retraining is not promised for every source change.

variants.title: Trace a removal through lineage
variants.context: Lineage answers both directions: what produced this model, and what depends on this source. When a source is corrected, expires, or becomes disallowed, resolve its identity to affected examples and releases, determine which model runs consumed them and where those artifacts are deployed, apply the governing response, and preserve an audit record without retaining prohibited payloads.
variants.prompt: An upstream system corrects six months of mislabeled transaction types. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Record the correction, its scope, the decision, and the evidence behind it.
List the model runs built on those releases and which of their artifacts are still serving traffic.
Decide per artifact whether to rebuild the dataset, retrain, restrict use, or accept a documented exception.
Map the corrected source records to the examples and releases that used the wrong values.

variants.hint: The same correction can justify different actions for different artifacts.
variants.explanation: The appropriate action depends on policy, model sensitivity, and whether the artifact is still used, so the system surfaces impact rather than acting on its own.

variants.title: Trace a removal through lineage
variants.context: Lineage answers both directions: what produced this model, and what depends on this source. When a source is corrected, expires, or becomes disallowed, resolve its identity to affected examples and releases, determine which model runs consumed them and where those artifacts are deployed, apply the governing response, and preserve an audit record without retaining prohibited payloads.
variants.prompt: A licensed corpus reaches the end of its permitted retention window. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Keep an auditable record of what expired, what was actioned, and who approved it.
Find the training runs that consumed those releases and the deployments still running their models.
Identify every example and dataset release that drew on the expiring corpus.
Apply the retention response the license requires for each affected artifact.

variants.hint: Retention is a policy contract with the same two directions as any other lineage question.
variants.explanation: Policy quality is traced through the same graph as data quality, which is why allowed uses and retention class belong in the manifest.

variants.title: Sort the quality layers
variants.context: Quality is several independent contracts, not one score. Structural quality covers parsing and identity. Statistical quality covers missingness, duplicates, balance, and change versus a known-good release. Semantic quality asks whether features and labels mean what the task assumes. Slice quality covers rare and safety-relevant segments. Policy quality covers allowed use, consent, sensitive data, and retention.
variants.prompt: Match each quality layer to what it validates.

pairs.label: Structural
pairs.detail: Required fields, types, ranges, parse success, referential integrity, and unique example IDs.

pairs.label: Statistical
pairs.detail: Missingness, duplicates, class balance, outliers, and change versus a known-good release.

pairs.label: Semantic
pairs.detail: Whether features and labels mean what the task assumes, including units, taxonomy, and point-in-time eligibility.

pairs.label: Slice
pairs.detail: Coverage and error-prone patterns for rare, safety-relevant, regional, device, or product segments.

pairs.label: Policy
pairs.detail: Allowed use, consent or license evidence, sensitive-data handling, access boundaries, and retention status.

variants.hint: One layer asks whether the row parses, another whether it is allowed to be here at all.
variants.explanation: The layers are validated independently so an aggregate average cannot hide a critical failure in one of them.

variants.title: Sort the quality layers
variants.context: Quality is several independent contracts, not one score. Structural quality covers parsing and identity. Statistical quality covers missingness, duplicates, balance, and change versus a known-good release. Semantic quality asks whether features and labels mean what the task assumes. Slice quality covers rare and safety-relevant segments. Policy quality covers allowed use, consent, sensitive data, and retention.
variants.prompt: A candidate release produces five findings. Match each finding to the quality layer it belongs to.

pairs.label: Two examples share the same example ID
The positive class fell from 8 percent to 3 percent against the last release
A weight column is recorded in pounds while the task assumes kilograms
The night-shift segment has 40 examples where the contract requires 2,000
One source has no recorded consent basis

variants.hint: Ask which contract each finding breaks, not how serious it feels.
variants.explanation: Routing a finding to its layer names the owner and the recovery action, which a single quality score cannot do.

variants.title: Sort the quality layers
variants.context: Quality is several independent contracts, not one score. Structural quality covers parsing and identity. Statistical quality covers missingness, duplicates, balance, and change versus a known-good release. Semantic quality asks whether features and labels mean what the task assumes. Slice quality covers rare and safety-relevant segments. Policy quality covers allowed use, consent, sensitive data, and retention.
variants.prompt: A second candidate produces five findings. Match each finding to the quality layer it belongs to.

pairs.label: A required timestamp column fails to parse in 2 percent of rows
Near-duplicate rows have risen sharply since the previous release
A label is set from an outcome that was only known a week after prediction time
Error rates are acceptable overall but poor for one low-bandwidth device class
A source's license forbids the redistribution the release plan assumes

variants.hint: Point-in-time eligibility is a question about meaning, not about parsing.
variants.explanation: A dataset can pass every structural check and still teach the wrong relationship, which is why semantic and slice layers stay separate.

variants.title: Decide the release gate outcome
variants.context: Every gate has an owner, threshold, scope, severity, and recovery action. Pass means the candidate can move to model evaluation. Quarantine keeps repairable data isolated. Block prevents release when a critical contract is violated.
variants.prompt: A candidate has 0.4 percent of rows with duplicate example IDs from a repeatable join defect. Everything else passes and the defect can be fixed by rebuilding the join. What should the gate do?
options: Block the release, because unique example IDs are a structural contract.
Pass the candidate and note the duplicate rate in the manifest for later review.
Quarantine the affected rows so the repairable defect stays isolated while the join is fixed.
optionFeedback: Blocking suits violations that cannot be repaired without new evidence, not a bounded and fixable join defect.
Passing a known identity defect lets it reach training, and a note in the manifest does not stop that.
Correct: quarantine keeps repairable data isolated without discarding the rest of the candidate.
variants.hint: Is the defect repairable from evidence already in hand?
variants.explanation: Quarantine is the disposition for repairable data. Pass and block are for candidates that are ready or that cannot be made ready.

variants.title: Decide the release gate outcome
variants.context: Every gate has an owner, threshold, scope, severity, and recovery action. Pass means the candidate can move to model evaluation. Quarantine keeps repairable data isolated. Block prevents release when a critical contract is violated.
variants.prompt: One of four sources in a candidate has no recorded consent basis or license evidence. Its rows are otherwise clean and it supplies 12 percent of the examples. What should the gate do?
options: Pass the release and open a follow-up task to collect the consent evidence.
Block the release, because a policy contract cannot be satisfied by data quality.
Quarantine the source's rows and release the remaining 88 percent immediately.
optionFeedback: A follow-up task does not prevent the training run that the signed manifest immediately authorizes.
Correct: allowed use is a critical contract, and a release signed without it misrepresents the dataset.
Dropping the source silently changes the population, and the gate outcome should be a decision an owner makes explicitly.
variants.hint: Which failures can never be repaired by rebuilding the data?
variants.explanation: Block when a critical contract is violated. Policy quality is independent of structural and statistical quality.

variants.title: Decide the release gate outcome
variants.context: Every gate has an owner, threshold, scope, severity, and recovery action. Pass means the candidate can move to model evaluation. Quarantine keeps repairable data isolated. Block prevents release when a critical contract is violated.
variants.prompt: Every gate passes. One feature's distribution moved, the owner traced it to a product launch, and slice coverage still meets the contract. What should the gate do?
options: Pass the candidate to model evaluation with the reviewed shift recorded in the manifest.
Block the release until the distribution returns to its previous range.
Quarantine the rows from the launched product so the release matches the old distribution.
optionFeedback: Correct: a shift is a prompt to investigate, and here the investigation finished and the contracts hold.
Blocking a valid population change would keep training on data the product no longer produces.
Removing the new population would make the release less representative of what the model will see.
variants.hint: A shift is a prompt to investigate, not proof of harm.
variants.explanation: Pass means the candidate can move to model evaluation. The reviewed explanation travels with the manifest so later readers can interpret it.

variants.title: Size the release decision
variants.context: Release decisions rest on counts. Reviewers size a queue from the rates of each defect, publishable volume is the candidate minus what quarantine holds, and a quarantine share is reported as a percentage of the candidate so it can be compared with a threshold.
variants.prompt: A candidate has 250,000 rows. Missing labels affect 1.2 percent of them and duplicate example IDs affect 0.8 percent. Ignoring any overlap, what is the upper bound on the rows a reviewer must handle?
variants.hint: An upper bound assumes no row has both defects.
variants.explanation: Summing the defect rates gives the largest queue the two problems can create, which is what a reviewer should plan capacity against.

mistakes.feedback: Counted only the missing labels and left out the duplicates.
Counted only the duplicates and left out the missing labels.

variants.title: Size the release decision
variants.context: Release decisions rest on counts. Reviewers size a queue from the rates of each defect, publishable volume is the candidate minus what quarantine holds, and a quarantine share is reported as a percentage of the candidate so it can be compared with a threshold.
variants.prompt: A candidate holds 80,000 examples and the gate quarantines 5 percent of them. How many examples remain publishable in the release?
variants.hint: Quarantine holds rows back; it does not add them.
variants.explanation: Publishable volume is the candidate minus everything quarantine holds, and the two counts must reconcile to the input.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the quarantined count instead of the publishable count.
Added the quarantined examples instead of subtracting them.

variants.title: Size the release decision
variants.context: Release decisions rest on counts. Reviewers size a queue from the rates of each defect, publishable volume is the candidate minus what quarantine holds, and a quarantine share is reported as a percentage of the candidate so it can be compared with a threshold.
variants.prompt: A candidate of 120,000 examples ends with 4,800 in quarantine. The gate blocks above 5 percent. What percentage of the candidate is quarantined?
variants.hint: Compare the held count with the whole candidate before comparing it with a threshold.
variants.explanation: A threshold is written as a share of the candidate, so the raw count has to be converted before the gate can be evaluated.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the raw count rather than the percentage the threshold is written in.
Divided the candidate by the quarantined count instead of the other way round.
